prompt: My MapLibre GL JS stylesheet has no `glyphs` property set at all, and my symbol layers have `text-font` set to a font name. Text labels are showing up, but in a generic font, not the one I specified. Is this a bug I need to fix, or expected behavior? What's actually happening?

The `text-font` array is treated exactly like a CSS `font-family` list: 1. **If the font name you put in `text-font` is available on the device (system font) or you have loaded it with `@font-face` / `document.fonts.load()`, the label will be drawn with that font.** 2. **If the name cannot be resolved, the browser picks the next available font in the list, eventually ending up with the generic “sans-serif” (or whatever the OS default is).** That is why you see a generic font instead of the one you expected. --- ## What’s really happening under the hood | Step | What MapLibre GL JS does | Why it works this way | |------|--------------------------|----------------------| | **Style parsing** | No `glyphs` field → *local-fonts mode* is activated (since GL JS v5.11). | The spec now treats the omission as a first-class feature, not an error. | | **`text-font` evaluation** | The array is turned into a CSS-style fallback list. Example: `["My Custom Font", "Noto Sans Regular", "sans-serif"]`. | Allows you to use any web-font you can load in the page. | | **Font loading** | - If you have a ``/`@font-face` rule that points to a font file whose **`font-family` name matches exactly** the string in `text-font`, the browser loads it.
- If you use the style’s `font-faces` property, GL JS will fetch those URLs and register them as `@font-face` rules automatically. | Gives you two ways to make the font available: (a) normal web-font loading, or (b) the style-driven `font-faces` mechanism. | | **Rendering** | For each glyph, TinySDF generates an SDF on-the-fly from the resolved font glyph outline. The result is drawn at any scale without needing a glyph-PBF server. | Keeps the map lightweight and works offline, but the visual result depends on the actual font that was resolved. | | **Fallback** | If the first name can’t be resolved, the next name in the list is tried, and so on, until the browser’s generic fallback is used. | Same behaviour as CSS `font-family`. | ### GL JS vs. MapLibre Native | Platform | `glyphs` required? | Local-fonts fallback | |----------|-------------------|----------------------| | **GL JS (≥ 5.11)** | Optional. If omitted, local-fonts mode is used. | ✅ Works out-of-the-box. | | **MapLibre Native** | **Required** – the style must contain a valid `glyphs` URL. | ❌ No fallback (as of v6.x). If you omit `glyphs`, the map will fail to render text on Native. | > **Takeaway:** If you need the same appearance on both GL JS *and* Native, keep a `glyphs` URL (even if you also use `font-faces`). If you only target GL JS, you can safely omit `glyphs` and rely on local fonts. --- ## Why you’re seeing a *generic* font 1. **The font file isn’t loaded** – you referenced `"My Fancy Font"` in `text-font` but never added a ``/`@font-face` rule for it, nor declared it in `font-faces`. The browser can’t find it, so it falls back. 2. **Name mismatch** – the `font-family` name inside the font file (or the `font-faces` entry) does not exactly match the string you wrote. Font names are case-sensitive and must include any weight/italic suffix you use (e.g., `"My Fancy Font Bold"` vs. `"My Fancy Font"`). 3. **CORS / loading error** – the font URL is blocked or returns 404, so the browser discards it and moves to the next fallback. 4. **Weight/italic handling** – GL JS only respects the *weight* keyword (`"Bold"`, `"Italic"`) that appears after the base name in the `text-font` array. If you rely on separate font files for bold/italic but don’t list them correctly, the generic fallback wins. --- ## How to make the intended font appear ### 1. Load the font via normal web-font mechanisms ```html ``` Then in your style: ```json { "type": "symbol", "layout": { "text-field": ["get", "name"], "text-font": ["My Fancy Font Bold", "My Fancy Font Regular", "sans-serif"] } } ``` *Result:* The browser resolves `"My Fancy Font Bold"` → the bold WOFF2 → TinySDF draws it. ### 2. Use the style-level `font-faces` property (GL JS ≥ 6.7) ```json { "font-faces": { "My Fancy Font": [ { "url": "https://example.com/fonts/MyFancyFont-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0000-FFFF"] }, { "url": "https://example.com/fonts/MyFancyFont-Bold.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0000-FFFF"] } ] }, "layers": [ { "id": "places", "type": "symbol", "layout": { "text-field": ["get", "name"], "text-font": ["My Fancy Font Bold", "My Fancy Font Regular", "sans-serif"] } } ] } ``` *What happens:* When the map loads, GL JS fetches the URLs, registers them as `@font-face` rules internally, and then resolves `text-font` exactly as above. No manual CSS needed. > **Tip:** `font-faces` works on Native as well (since Android 11.13 / iOS 6.18). If you plan to share the same style between GL JS and Native, prefer `font-faces` over external CSS. ### 3. Verify the name matches - Open the font file in a tool (e.g., FontForge, `ttx`, or even Chrome DevTools → “Fonts” panel) and check the **Family name**. - Use that exact string in `text-font`. If you want a weight variant, add the weight keyword after the family name (e.g., `"My Fancy Font Bold"`). Do **not** include the weight inside the family name unless the font file itself declares it that way. ### 4. Check loading errors Open the browser console and look for messages like: ``` Failed to load font: https://example.com/fonts/MyFancyFont-Regular.ttf (status: 404) Unable to load glyph range ... No bug to fix—just the expected local-fonts workflow.

Description: implicit — offline/local fonts on MapLibre Native, not GL JS
prompt: I'm building an offline map app with MapLibre Native on Android and want labels to render in local device fonts without running a glyphs server. What's the right way to configure this?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
## TL;DR  

*MapLibre Native on Android cannot run without a **glyphs** URL, but you can make the map draw almost everything from fonts that you ship with the APK.*  

1. **Bundle the TTF/OTF files you want to use** (e.g. Noto Sans, Noto Sans CJK SC, Noto Sans Arabic, …) in `app/src/main/assets/fonts/`.  
2. **Add a `font-faces` section to your style** that points at those assets with `asset://` URLs (or `file:///android_asset/…`).  
3. **Keep a tiny glyph-server stub** (or copy the pre-built glyph PBF tree for the few Latin/Latin-extended glyphs you really need) and point the style’s `glyphs` field at it.  
4. **Do NOT set `localIdeographFontFamily`** – that option only exists in GL JS.  
5. **Load the style** exactly as you would for any offline map; the native runtime will use the bundled fonts for every script that HarfBuzz can shape (Arabic, Hebrew, Devanagari, Thai, etc.) and will fall back to the local glyph PBFs for the remaining code-points (Latin, numbers, punctuation).  

Below is a complete, step-by-step recipe, plus the “gotchas” you’ll hit the first time you try it.

---

## 1. Why you still need a `glyphs` URL

| SDK | What happens if `glyphs` is omitted? |
|-----|---------------------------------------|
| **MapLibre GL JS ≥ 5.11** | Text is rendered locally with TinySDF; the `glyphs` field is optional. |
| **MapLibre Native (Android, iOS)** | The style parser **requires** a `glyphs` template. If it is missing the map will fail to load (`StyleParseException: missing glyphs URL`). The native code does **not** have the TinySDF fallback that GL JS added. |

So the *only* way to go completely offline on Native is to **provide a glyph source** that the runtime can reach – even if that source only contains a handful of ranges.

### Two practical ways to satisfy the requirement

| Option | What you ship | When to use it |
|--------|---------------|----------------|
| **Copy the pre-built glyph PBF tree** (e.g. `fonts.openmaptiles.org` or the `openmaptiles/fonts` repo) into your APK’s `assets/glyphs/` folder. | All Latin-based ranges (0-255, 256-511, …) are already tiny (≈ 10 KB each). | You want a *real* SDF rendering for Latin text (sharp at any zoom) and you don’t mind a few hundred kilobytes in the APK. |
| **Serve an empty-glyph stub** (a tiny 0-byte PBF that returns “no glyphs”). | Only needed if you are happy to let the native renderer fall back to the bundled fonts for *every* script, including Latin. | You have a brand-font that already contains every glyph you need, or you are OK with the native engine rasterising the font on-the-fly (the engine will still ask for a PBF, get an empty one, and then use the `font-faces` font). |

The **recommended** approach for most offline apps is the first one: copy the existing glyph PBFs. They are small, battle-tested, and you avoid a “missing glyph” warning in the log.

---

## 2. Bundle the fonts you want to use

### 2.1 Add the files to the APK

```
app/
 └─ src/
     └─ main/
         └─ assets/
             ├─ fonts/
             │   ├─ NotoSans-Regular.ttf
             │   ├─ NotoSans-Bold.ttf
             │   ├─ NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf
             │   ├─ NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf
             │   └─ NotoSansCJKsc-Regular.otf
             └─ glyphs/
                 └─ (copy of the glyph-pbf tree, see step 3)
```

*Tip:* If you use Gradle’s `android.assets.srcDirs` you can keep the fonts in a separate module and copy them automatically during the build.

### 2.2 Declare them in the style’s `font-faces`

```json
{
  "version": 8,
  "glyphs": "asset://glyphs/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf",
  "font-faces": {
    "Noto Sans Regular": [
      {
        "url": "asset://fonts/NotoSans-Regular.ttf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+0000-00FF", "U+0100-024F"]   // Latin + Latin-Extended
      }
    ],
    "Noto Sans Arabic": [
      {
        "url": "asset://fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+0600-06FF", "U+0750-077F"]
      }
    ],
    "Noto Sans Devanagari": [
      {
        "url": "asset://fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+0900-097F"]
      }
    ],
    "Noto Sans CJK SC": [
      {
        "url": "asset://fonts/NotoSansCJKsc-Regular.otf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+4E00-9FFF", "U+3400-4DBF"]
      }
    ]
  },
  "layers": [
    {
      "id": "place-labels",
      "type": "symbol",
      "source": "osm",
      "source-layer": "place",
      "layout": {
        "text-field": ["get", "name"],
        "text-font": [
          "Noto Sans CJK SC",
          "Noto Sans Arabic",
          "Noto Sans Devanagari",
          "Noto Sans Regular"
        ],
        "text-size": 12
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

*Important points*

* **`url` must be a scheme the native runtime can resolve.** `asset://` is interpreted by the Android native library as “load from the APK assets folder”.  
* **`unicode-range` is optional** – you can omit it if the font file contains only the script you care about.  
* **The order in `text-font` is a fallback list**. The first entry that contains the requested code-point (or that the glyph server can supply) wins.  

---

## 3. Provide a (tiny) glyph-PBF tree for the `glyphs` field

### 3.1 Copy an existing tree

The easiest way is to clone the public OpenMapTiles font repo and copy the relevant folders:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/openmaptiles/fonts.git
# The tree looks like: fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf
# Example: fonts/Noto%20Sans%20Regular/0-255.pbf
cp -R fonts/* app/src/main/assets/glyphs/
```

*Why the `asset://` scheme works*: The native runtime builds a `FileSource` that knows how to read `asset://` URLs from the APK. No network request is made.

### 3.2 (Optional) Trim the tree

If you really want to keep the APK size down, you can delete the ranges you never use (e.g. 256-511 for Latin-Extended-A, 512-767 for Latin-Extended-B, etc.). The native engine will simply request a missing range, get a 404, and then fall back to the `font-faces` font you declared. The log will contain a line like:

```
[WARN] Unable to load glyph range 256-511.pbf, rendering locally instead.
```

That warning is harmless – it just tells you that the glyph PBF was not found and the engine used the bundled font.

---

```kotlin
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)

        // 1️⃣ Initialise the MapLibre SDK (once per process)
        MapLibre.getInstance(this)

        // 2️⃣ Create the MapView
        mapView = MapView(this)
        setContentView(mapView)

        // 3️⃣ Build the MapOptions – note we do NOT set a remote style URL
        val options = MapOptions()
            .withStyleUri("asset://style/offline-style.json") // <-- our bundled style
            .withResourceOptions(
                ResourceOptions.Builder()
                    .withAccessToken("")               // not needed for offline
                    .build()
            )
            .withGlyphsRasterizationMode(
                GlyphsRasterizationMode.LOCAL // <-- tells Native to rasterise glyphs from font-faces when a PBF is missing
            )

        // 4️⃣ Create the map
        mapView.getMapAsync { mapboxMap ->
            mapboxMap.loadStyleUri(options.styleUri) {
                // style is loaded – you can now add sources, layers, etc.
            }
        }
    }

    override fun onStart() {
        super.onStart()
        mapView.onStart()
    }

    override fun onStop() {
        super.onStop()
        mapView.onStop()
    }

    // … (onResume, onPause, onDestroy, etc.)
}
```

### What the code does

| Line | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `withStyleUri("asset://style/offline-style.json")` | Loads the JSON you edited in step 2 from the APK assets. |
| `withGlyphsRasterizationMode(GlyphsRasterizationMode.LOCAL)` | **New in MapLibre Native 11.13** – tells the renderer to fall back to the `font-faces` fonts when a glyph PBF cannot be found. This is the native analogue of GL JS’s “local-font fallback”. |
| No `setRTLTextPlugin` call needed – the native engine uses HarfBuzz for Arabic, Hebrew, etc. |

> **Note:** `GlyphsRasterizationMode.LOCAL` is *optional* but highly recommended for offline use. If you omit it, the engine will simply skip characters whose PBF is missing, leaving blanks in the label.

---

## 5. Special script handling

| Script | How it is rendered on Native (offline) | What you must provide |
|--------|----------------------------------------|-----------------------|
| **Latin, numbers, punctuation** | Prefer the glyph-PBF SDF (sharp at any zoom). If the PBF is missing, the engine rasterises the `font-faces` font (thanks to `LOCAL` mode). | Either copy the standard glyph PBFs **or** rely on the rasterisation fallback. |
